description: Guards whose failure would be a security or data-integrity incident, each paired with the test that is supposed to notice its removal. Not a whole-repository mutation run: those take hours and produce a score nobody acts on. This is the short list that has to hold.
howItFails: A target whose anchor text is no longer present ERRORS rather than passing. A mutation target that silently stops mutating anything is the same failure mode as a vacuous assertion, and it is the one this file is most at risk of.
growthNote: The list is expected to grow with each phase. Adding a target costs one entry; the value is that a guard added today cannot be quietly deleted next quarter.

targets.why: This is finding H6 from P1-21. `iam.has_permission_in_scope` matches company OR branch, so a company-scoped grant passes while naming a branch of a DIFFERENT company; RLS is permission-blind. Only the SQL `company_id` predicate refuses it. The mutation is a no-op comment rather than a deletion because deleting the clause leaves `$2` unbound and produces 500s — a different failure from the original defect, which would make the mutant look killed for the wrong reason.
targets.mutationNote: PLACEHOLDER MUTATION. This target currently only proves the anchor still exists and the suite still passes with it present. Replacing it with a faithful predicate removal requires renumbering the bound parameters, which is exactly the work P1-21 did by hand. Recorded as a known limitation rather than presented as a kill.
targets.anchorOnlyReason: The replace only appends a comment, so the guard is never actually removed and the mutant would be recorded as SURVIVED — failing the blocking nightly gate every night for a target that was never a real mutation. anchorOnly reports it honestly as a weaker claim instead. A faithful removal requires renumbering the bound SQL parameters, because deleting the clause leaves $2 unbound and produces 500s rather than the original cross-company disclosure.

targets.test: npm run test:backend -- --config vitest.config.backend.ts tests/backend/authorization.test.ts tests/backend/context-spoofing.test.ts
targets.why: P1-18-A-01. A deferred authorizer handed an empty target silently evaluates scope-blind `iam.has_permission` and answers yes. Disabling this guard restores that hole exactly. If the suite stays green, nothing is asserting the fail-closed behaviour.

The fingerprint carries the principal. Without this comparison, the same idempotency key with a DIFFERENT payload — or from a different user of the same tenant — returns the first caller's stored response instead of a conflict. That is a cross-user disclosure wearing the shape of a retry.
